title: Gap width, wavelength and diffraction experiments
prior_knowledge_summary: Diffraction is wave spreading through a gap or around an obstacle.
Wavelength can be read as the spacing between adjacent wavefronts.
Topic 7 established wavefronts, wavelength and progressive-wave language.
new_learning: Qualitative dependence of diffraction on gap width relative to wavelength.

learning_outcomes.statement: Show an understanding of experiments that demonstrate diffraction, including the qualitative effect of gap width relative to wavelength.

evidence_basis.note: No primary-mapped P2 leaf currently covers this outcome. No P1 lesson assignment inferred.

blocks.title: Which gap makes waves fan out most?
content: Straight water wavefronts approach three openings. One is much wider than their spacing, one is about the same width, and one is narrower. Which opening produces the widest spread behind the barrier?
The answer is not set by gap width alone. We must compare the gap with the wavelength.

figure.purpose: Create the need to compare gap width with wavelength.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper prediction sketch with the same incoming water-wave spacing meeting three gaps labelled wider than, similar to and narrower than that spacing. Leave outgoing regions blank for prediction.
figure.alt_text: Equal-wavelength water waves approach three gaps of different widths.

blocks.title: The comparison needs wavelength

controlled_definitions.displayed_content: the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase
the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle

content: Wavelength is the minimum distance between two adjacent points on a wave that are in phase. In a ripple-tank view, adjacent wavefronts show this distance clearly.
Diffraction is the spreading of waves as they pass through a gap or around an obstacle. To predict the amount of spreading at a gap, compare its width with the wavelength.

figure.purpose: Show exactly which two lengths are compared.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn measurement layout with wavelength marked between adjacent straight wavefronts and gap width marked across one aperture using distinct colours and sparse labels.
figure.alt_text: A diagram marks wavelength between adjacent wavefronts and width across a gap.

blocks.title: Comparable sizes give strong spreading
content: When the gap width is comparable with the wavelength, the emerging wavefronts spread strongly. A top view can look close to semicircular wavefronts from the opening.
When the gap is many wavelengths wide, most of each emerging wavefront continues nearly straight. There is still spreading near the edges, but the overall change of direction is smaller.

figure.purpose: Compare strong and weak diffraction using matched wavefront diagrams.
figure.brief: Two-panel teacher sketch using equal wavelength: a gap about one wavelength wide with strongly curved outgoing fronts, and a gap several wavelengths wide with mostly straight outgoing fronts plus edge spreading.
figure.alt_text: A one-wavelength gap gives stronger spreading than a many-wavelength gap.

blocks.title: A fair ripple-tank comparison
content: Keep the water depth and vibrator frequency fixed so the wavelength stays fixed. Send straight wavefronts toward an adjustable gap. Observe or sketch the wavefront shape after the gap, then reduce the gap width and repeat.
A fair comparison changes the gap width while keeping the incoming wavelength fixed. Stronger curvature and waves reaching farther into the side regions show stronger diffraction.

figure.purpose: Teach the experimental control and observation sequence.
figure.brief: Four-step ripple-tank sequence: set straight waves, measure wavefront spacing, set gap width, trace outgoing fronts. Highlight fixed depth and frequency and changed gap width.
figure.alt_text: A ripple-tank procedure changes gap width while keeping wavelength fixed.

blocks.title: The same gap can behave differently
content: Now keep the opening fixed and compare two wavelengths. The longer wavelength is more comparable with the gap width, so it spreads more. The shorter wavelength is small compared with the same gap, so it travels more nearly straight through.

This explains why sound can spread noticeably through a doorway while visible light usually gives little obvious spreading there. Their wavelengths are enormously different compared with the doorway width. This is a wavelength comparison, not a claim that only sound diffracts.

figure.purpose: Re-explain the ratio idea by holding the gap fixed and changing wavelength.
figure.brief: Two-panel fixed-doorway comparison: widely spaced wavefronts spreading strongly and closely spaced wavefronts spreading weakly. Add a crossed-out note saying only sound diffracts.
figure.alt_text: At one fixed opening, longer-wavelength waves spread more than shorter-wavelength waves.

blocks.title: Use a relative comparison, not a slogan
content: It is tempting to say that a small gap always gives more diffraction. That can fail because small has no meaning until it is compared with wavelength. A 2 cm gap is wide for a 1 mm wavelength but narrow for a 10 cm wavelength.

Use this reasoning route: identify the wavelength, identify the gap width, compare them, then predict the spreading. Comparable sizes give marked diffraction. A gap many wavelengths wide gives less diffraction. No interference or fringe argument is needed.

figure.purpose: Consolidate the four-step qualitative prediction method and correct absolute-width reasoning.
figure.brief: Hand-drawn flow chart: wavelength, gap width, compare, predict curvature. Include two number-line examples for a 2 cm gap with 1 mm and 10 cm wavelengths, without calculation formulas.
figure.alt_text: A flow chart compares wavelength and gap width before predicting diffraction.

concepts_taught: qualitative dependence of diffraction on gap width relative to wavelength
misconceptions_addressed: A small gap always causes strong diffraction regardless of wavelength.
Only sound diffracts at everyday openings.
skills_students_can_now_use: Predict relative diffraction from gap width and wavelength.
